title: ADR: SLA composition for staged rollouts and heterogeneous dependency tolerances
author: Maya Patel
body:
Summary:
This ADR defines how Redwood composes service-level agreements (SLAs) across staged rollouts that interact with heterogeneous downstream dependency tolerances. It establishes a deterministic algorithm for SLA composition, a matrix for allowed degradation modes during canary and ramp phases, and mandatory telemetry/alerting hooks for rollout automation and rollback criteria.

Context and motivation:
- We frequently deploy changes to the inference control plane, routing logic, and model variants using staged rollouts (canary -> ramp -> global).
- Downstream services (cache, KV store, dedicated GPU pools, third-party indexers) each expose different latency distributions and error semantics.
- Customers require end-to-end SLAs for latency and availability even while we perform progressive rollouts and feature gating.
- Existing practice created ambiguity about who compensates for downstream variance and when automatic rollback should trigger. This ADR standardizes those decisions.

Goals:
1. Provide a clear, reproducible method to compute end-to-end SLA exposures for rolling releases.
2. Define allowable degradation envelopes during each rollout phase and tie them to rollout policies.
3. Require concrete telemetry and alert thresholds to enable automated safe-fail or rollback.
4. Ensure ownership and communication responsibilities are explicit for incidents during rollouts.

Decision (what we will do):
- SLA Composition Model: we adopt a tiered composition model where end-to-end SLA is computed as a weighted composition of component SLIs using request-path weights observed in production. Weighting rules:
  - Use sampled path traces over the prior 7 days to compute path frequency (min 1000 samples).
  - For each path, compute P95 latency and availability for each component.
  - End-to-end P95 = weighted sum of component medians plus measured inter-component queueing delta (see formula below).

- Allowed Degradation Matrix by Rollout Phase:
  1) Canary (<=1% traffic): Allowed latency increase per-path: +20% absolute P95 (capped at +200ms). Availability drop allowed: up to 0.3 percentage points.  2) Ramp (1%–25%): Allowed latency increase per-path: +10% absolute P95 (capped at +100ms). Availability drop allowed: up to 0.1 percentage points.  3) Global (>25%): No allowed degradation beyond baseline SLO; must meet standard SLAs.

- Component-level tolerances: each dependent service must publish a tolerance profile (JSON schema, see "SLA Profile" below) and an emergency fallback contract (e.g., degraded mode with cached responses, reduced token-rate, or best-effort responses). If a component cannot provide a tolerance profile, it defaults to conservative mode: deny rollout beyond Canary.

- Rollout Policy Enforcement:
  - Canary: deployer must attach a rollout record with target metric (P95 latency, error-rate) and thresholds. Canary may proceed if telemetry shows <50% of allowed degradation in first 30 minutes.
  - Ramp: automated gates evaluate 5-minute windows; if metrics exceed phase thresholds for 3 consecutive windows, an automated rollback (or pause) is triggered and on-call is paged.
  - Global: requires explicit approval from service owner and SRE after observing at least 48 hours within Ramp without alerts.

Operational procedures and telemetry requirements:
1) Required telemetry: trace sampling (1:1000 min), per-path P50/P95/P99, per-component error-rate, per-route request volume, and queue/processing time deltas.
2) Alert rules (examples):
   - Canary critical: end-to-end P95 > allowed_canary_P95 for 2 consecutive 5m windows -> immediate rollback and page SRE (pager duty).
   - Ramp warning: end-to-end error-rate > baseline_error_rate + 0.05 for 15m -> pause ramp and create incident channel.
3) Dashboards: each rollout must instantiate a temporary rollout dashboard (auto-created by the deployment pipeline) that contains the SLA composition table, path breakdown pie, and top contributing components.
4) Post-rollout review: within 5 business days, delivery team must open a short retro summarizing measured deltas, incidents, and any manual mitigations.

SLA Profile (JSON schema reference - textual):
- component_name: string
- owner: team name
- baseline_p95_ms: number
- baseline_availability_pct: number
- fallback_mode: one of ["cached-response", "reduced-throughput", "best-effort", "reject-fast"]
- max_allowed_delta_ms_canary: number
- max_allowed_delta_ms_ramp: number
- contact_oncall: rota id

Example SLA Composition Table (per-route, for human review):
| Route | Path weight (%) | Component A P95 (ms) | Component B P95 (ms) | Inter-component delta (ms) | Composed P95 (ms) | Allowed during phase |
|-------|-----------------|----------------------|----------------------|----------------------------|-------------------|---------------------|
| /v1/generate | 62 | 45 | 120 | 25 | 252 | Canary +200ms |
| /v1/embed | 25 | 30 | 40 | 10 | 80 | Ramp +100ms |
| /health | 13 | 5 | 8 | 2 | 15 | No degradation |

Rollback and mitigation matrix (short):
1) Exceeded canary critical -> immediate rollback to previous stable version, invalidate new routing metadata, flush small-prefix caches, notify customers (if applicable).
2) Ramp transient spike -> pause ramp, reduce traffic to last safe percentage, invoke component-level fallback contract (e.g., switch to cached-response), escalate to component owner.
3) Silent degradation observed in low-volume paths -> schedule controlled test and canary re-run targeted at affected paths.

Ownership and communication:
- Service owner: accountable for rollout approval and for publishing component SLA profile.
- SRE: sets sensible defaults for alert thresholds, maintains rollout automation scripts, and owns rollback automation.
- Product/Customer Success: must be notified for any global rollback that could affect paid SLAs.

Migration and constraints:
- Short-term: all active services must publish a basic SLA profile within 60 days of this ADR. Deployment pipeline will reject ramp beyond 1% for services without profiles.
- Long-term: integrate SLA composition into cost and routing decisions (Optimize) and feed into canary traffic shaping.

Consequences (pros/cons):
Pros:
- Deterministic, measurable approach reduces ambiguity during rollouts.
- Enables safer automation for staged rollouts and faster detection of regressions.
- Sets clear accountability for downstream components.
Cons/Risks:
- Additional operational burden for teams to publish and maintain SLA profiles.
- Weighting and sampling assumptions may misestimate rare but high-impact tails. We mitigate via periodic synthetic load tests.

Open items and extensions:
- Define precise formula for inter-component queueing delta (owner: eng-serving-runtime, due 2026-03-01).
- Determine retention policy of sampled traces for path weighting (proposal: 30 days, subject to telemetry storage cost review).
- Explore automatic compensation policies for customers if composed SLA is missed during a rollout window.

References and related pages:
- Cross-service fallback topology guidelines (infra-standards)
- End-to-end SLI composition playbook (observability-standards)
- Rollout automation runbooks (eng-platform/runbooks)

Approval:
- Approved by: Maya Patel (author), Daniel Kim (SRE reviewer), Priya Shah (runtime review)
- Date approved: 2026-02-15

Appendix (formulas):
- Weighted end-to-end P95 = sum_over_paths( weight_path * (sum_components P50_component + inter_component_delta_path ) ) + path_tail_adjustment.
- For purposes of rollout gating we evaluate the computed P95 against the phase-allowed P95 and also the measured P99 to detect emerging tails.

Notes:
- This ADR is operational immediately for all new rollouts. Existing active rollouts should adopt these rules on their next planned ramp step or within 30 days, whichever is sooner.
